item.title: Kanye West’s Alice Merton Sample Case Dismissed After Settlement Deal
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Kanye West's settlement with Alice Merton removes a March trial date, while the court leaves room to reopen the case.
item.content:encoded:
Kanye West‘s sample dispute with Alice Merton has moved off the trial calendar after the two sides reached a settlement.

A federal judge dismissed the case without prejudice while leaving a 90-day window to reopen it if the deal runs into trouble.

Judge Fernando L. Aenlle-Rocha issued the dismissal order and canceled every remaining deadline. Merton and her companies had notified the court six days earlier that they had reached an agreement with Ye and Yeezy Record Label.

The November 6 notice said the settlement would resolve the entire case once its obligations were completed.

It anticipated approximately 30 to 45 days of performance after the written agreement was signed.

“Upon full performance, the Parties will file a stipulation dismissing the entire action with prejudice,” Merton’s lawyers wrote. The filing did not disclose a dollar amount or spell out those obligations.

Merton sued over “Gun To My Head,” alleging the Vultures 2 track incorporated her 2022 song “Blindside” despite her refusal to authorize it. The German singer said her family’s history as Holocaust survivors and Ye’s antisemitic statements drove that refusal.

Her complaint followed a clearance request sent to BMG in February 2024. She declined permission the following month, but alleged Ye released the song that August anyway.

The case had recently produced a ruling keeping references to antisemitism and the Holocaust in the lawsuit. Ye’s lawyers sought to remove those allegations, arguing they were unrelated to the copyright dispute.

Aenlle-Rocha rejected that request in October because the allegations helped explain Merton’s refusal. Ye’s defense also challenged the evidence supporting her infringement claim.

The new dismissal allows either side to request reopening within 90 days by explaining why settlement remains incomplete, what still needs doing and when completion is expected. The parties can instead file their agreed dismissal with prejudice within that period.

“All deadlines governing this action are VACATED,” Aenlle-Rocha wrote in the order. The settlement notice had also asked to remove a November 20 hearing on the defendants’ pending summary-judgment motion from the court’s calendar.

The now-canceled trial had been scheduled for March 15, 2027.

item.title: Lionel Richie Returns To Vegas After Heart Procedure
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Lionel Richie resumes his Wynn residency after weeks away for recovery, with more Las Vegas performances on the calendar.
item.content:encoded:
Lionel Richie resumed his Las Vegas residency Wednesday after a heart procedure interrupted his touring schedule, bringing the 77-year-old R&B star back to Encore Theater at Wynn.

The November 11 performance opened his latest “King of Hearts” run. Rather than avoid the health concerns that surrounded his absence, Richie addressed them directly and thanked the audience for checking on him.

“I’m back! I don’t know where I was, but I’m back!” Richie said, according to the Las Vegas Review-Journal’s account from the show.

Richie had stepped away from performing after undergoing treatment for atrial fibrillation in September. His representative said the procedure was successful, but the singer needed time to recover before returning to work.

The break followed canceled concerts with Earth, Wind & Fire. Earlier in the year, he fell ill during a June performance, and an August hospital visit brought another interruption to his concert plans.

“I feel just fine, thank you all so much for caring about me,” Richie told the Las Vegas crowd.

Wednesday’s set drew from both his solo recordings and his years with the Commodores. It also included a duet with footage of Kenny Rogers on “Lady,” the song Richie wrote for the country star.

Richie’s career spans the Commodores’ soul ballads and some of the biggest crossover records of the 1980s. He wrote “Easy,” “Still,” and “Three Times a Lady” during his time with the group before building his own catalog.

His solo hits include “Hello” and “Dancing on the Ceiling,” while his songwriting work also includes the 1985 charity single “We Are the World.” His honors include four Grammys, an Oscar and induction into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2022.

His work has extended beyond the stage. Richie produced the documentary “The Greatest Night in Pop,” which premiered at the Sundance Film Festival in 2024 and earned three Primetime Emmy nominations.

Las Vegas has been part of that later career for a decade. Richie began his first headlining residency there in April 2016, years before the current “King of Hearts” production.

Wynn’s calendar lists his next performances for November 13 and 14, followed by January 8 and 9.

item.title: Prince’s Former Lawyers Put Artist Ownership At Center Of Paisley Park Symposium
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Prince's Emancipation anniversary brings his former attorneys and collaborators together to revisit his fight for control.
item.content:encoded:
Prince‘s fight to control his music will bring two of his former lawyers back into the conversation at Paisley Park next week.

The inaugural Emancipation 30 Retrospective and Symposium pairs the album’s anniversary with discussions about ownership, creative independence and constitutional freedoms.

The November 19-21 gathering in Chanhassen, Minnesota, is co-hosted by Mayte Garcia and L. Londell McMillan. McMillan will moderate a Friday panel featuring U.S. District Judge Jerry W. Blackwell, another former Prince attorney, alongside civil-rights and First Amendment voices.

“It is an honor to produce and continue the legacy of freedom, justice and innovation with Emancipation 30. We will engage in deep discussions and honor Prince, his music, intellect and vision for a free and just global society. Prince deserves a salute not only for his incomparable talents and music but also his loving and courageous humanity,” McMillan said.

Garcia, McMillan and recording engineer Hans-Martin Buff will also participate in Thursday’s livestreamed conversation about the Emancipation years.

The album arrived on November 19, 1996, through NPG Records and EMI after Prince’s contentious relationship with Warner Bros. His final album of new material for Warner, Chaos and Disorder, had arrived that July, following the March release of his Girl 6 soundtrack.

Prince made his independence audible, assembling 36 tracks across three discs that each ran precisely an hour. The collection moved between styles rather than squeezing his output into a conventional single-disc release, with songs including “The Holy River” and “Somebody’s Somebody.”

The launch also reached television audiences through a Paisley Park concert carried simultaneously by BET, MTV and VH1 on November 12, 1996. The subsequent Jam of the Year tour included musicians Kirk Johnson, Morris Hayes and Mike Scott, who are returning for the anniversary program.

Prince was 57 when he died at Paisley Park on April 21, 2016. The Midwest Medical Examiner’s Office later determined that an accidental overdose of fentanyl caused his death.

Questions about control continued after his death, with a 2022 estate agreement dividing assets between Prince Legacy LLC and Prince Oat Holdings LLC.

That agreement followed six years of proceedings over an estate valued at roughly $156 million.

The new symposium includes a San Antonio concert-film screening and free Saturday community activities, giving the weekend room beyond its industry discussions.

New Power Generation will perform music from Emancipation during Saturday’s anniversary concert.

Saturday’s New Power Generation performance is scheduled to begin at 8 P.M. Central, with doors opening at 4 P.M.

item.title: Diddy Accuser Drops White Party Assault Lawsuit With Prejudice
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Diddy's former White Party security guard abandons his civil case as a separate fight over his lawyers' exit remains on file.
item.content:encoded:
Diddy‘s White Party sexual assault accuser is dropping his federal lawsuit with prejudice, according to a new filing in the case brought by a former security guard. The notice covers the action against the mogul and the companies named alongside him.

The plaintiff filed the notice in Manhattan federal court, with another copy entered November 13. It gives no explanation for the decision and discloses no payment or settlement terms.

The notice of voluntary dismissal states that the action “is voluntarily dismissed with prejudice.” That designation prevents the plaintiff from bringing the same claims again.

“Counsel for Plaintiff have discussed this matter with counsel who acknowledge and consent to this submission,” the filing states. It lists attorneys Antigone Curis and Mark Cuccaro and includes an unfilled space for a judge’s signature.

The case began in October 2024, and an amended complaint followed on December 10 of that year. In his amended complaint, the man alleged Diddy drugged and sexually assaulted him while he worked security at an August 2007 party at the rapper’s East Hampton property.

Diddy has denied sexually assaulting anyone. His lawyers also challenged this particular lawsuit’s legal basis, arguing that the New York City gender-motivated violence law invoked by the plaintiff did not reach alleged conduct outside the city.

The defense raised additional objections about the filing deadline and the claims against Diddy’s companies. The plaintiff sought compensatory and punitive damages without specifying a dollar amount in the amended complaint.

The lawsuit also produced a dispute over anonymity. Judge Naomi Reice Buchwald rejected the plaintiff’s request to proceed under a pseudonym in April 2025, and he appealed; the court subsequently stayed the case pending the appeals.

More recently, it became another front in Sher Tremonte’s effort to leave Diddy’s civil cases. The firm moved to withdraw in October, and Buchwald ordered the defendants to respond to its request.

That order also addressed the firm’s bid to retain case files over unpaid expenses. The new dismissal notice does not describe how those attorney-fee issues will be resolved.

Buchwald’s October 23 order set November 23 as the defendants’ response deadline.

item.title: Raz B’s Infant Son’s Death Ruled Accidental, Medical Examiner Says
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Raz B and Mona Li's infant son Astro died accidentally, according to a new report citing the Fulton County Medical Examiner.
item.content:encoded:
Raz B and his wife Mona Li’s infant son, Astro, died accidentally, according to a new report citing the Fulton County Medical Examiner. The finding comes two months after the B2K singer’s family announced the loss of their three-month-old child.

The medical examiner confirmed asphyxia caused by an obstructed airway and also confirmed the accidental manner of death.

The county’s September 10 public notice had listed the cause as pending investigation. That notice recorded Astro’s death on September 8 and an autopsy the following day.

The family’s spokesperson, David Robinson, confirmed the loss in September. At the time, the family described Astro’s death as unexpected and asked for space to grieve.

“The family asks for privacy as they navigate this difficult time and appreciates your love and support in advance,” a statement shared with PEOPLE said. It did not disclose a cause of death.

AllHipHop previously reported the family’s loss in September. Raz B had announced Astro’s arrival through Instagram in May.

The family had shared the lead-up to Astro’s birth while Raz B was back on the road with B2K. In April, Mona Li marked the end of the group’s Boys 4 Life tour with Bow Wow, praising her husband’s determination to keep performing for their family.

By May, those updates had shifted from the stage to the hospital. Raz B posted that they were preparing to welcome another son and thanked his wife for her strength during the pregnancy. He followed with a tribute recognizing her role as a mother and partner.

Raz B rose to prominence alongside Omarion, J-Boog and Lil’ Fizz as a member of B2K.

item.title: Hip-Hop and Gambling Sponsorships: How Brand Deals, Streaming Rules and Fan Trust Intersect
item.dc:creator: Staff Writer
item.description: Hip-hop stars are expanding their business empires through online gambling sponsorships. From Drake’s Stake partnership to sponsored livestreams, these deals bring major opportunities alongside advertising restrictions, fan trust concerns and reputation risks.
item.content:encoded:
For today’s biggest rap stars, music is just one part of a much broader business. Sneaker collaborations, fashion collections, technology partnerships and lifestyle brands have become important sources of income alongside streaming and live performances. Successful artists increasingly use their cultural influence to build partnerships with companies looking to connect with highly engaged audiences across Instagram, YouTube and streaming platforms.

Online gambling companies have also become part of this growing sponsorship landscape, recognizing the marketing potential of influential figures in hip-hop. One of the most recognizable examples is Drake’s long-running partnership with Stake, which has brought together music, celebrity culture and digital entertainment through social media content, livestreams and promotional campaigns.

Such collaborations demonstrate how hip-hop artists have evolved beyond traditional music careers into influential brand ambassadors. For gambling operators, partnerships with established performers offer opportunities to increase brand awareness and reach new audiences. For artists, they represent another way to expand their commercial portfolios and strengthen their presence in the digital entertainment industry.

Why Gambling Brands Partner With Hip-Hop Artists

Hip-hop has become a powerful influence on fashion, entertainment, social media and consumer culture. For brands looking to reach younger, digitally engaged audiences, partnerships with established rappers offer a way to connect with communities that traditional advertising often struggles to reach. An artist’s endorsement can make a brand more recognizable and relatable, particularly when the collaboration feels like a natural extension of their public image.

This influence has attracted companies from industries beyond music, including fashion, technology, sports and online gambling. Casino operators, in particular, compete for visibility in a crowded digital market where attracting attention and building brand recognition are major marketing challenges. By collaborating with hip-hop artists, these companies can introduce their platforms to new audiences through music videos, social media campaigns, sponsored content and live events.

A rapper might introduce millions of followers to a gambling brand, but factors such as licensing, payment methods, promotional terms and withdrawal conditions still require independent consideration. This is where industry information platforms become relevant. In Canada, for example, casinocanada.com  provides information about online casino operators, available bonuses and payment options, helping readers understand the services that gambling brands advertise.

The distinction between promotion and independent research is especially important in an industry subject to advertising restrictions and consumer protection requirements.

From Traditional Endorsements to Digital Partnerships

Endorsements used to mean a TV spot or a billboard. Today, a gambling partnership can take several forms:

  • Paid social media posts: sponsored content on Instagram, TikTok, X or YouTube that promotes a brand directly to the artist’s followers.
  • Branded content: videos, behind-the-scenes clips or online series produced together with the brand, where the product is built into the story.
  • Marketing campaigns: appearances in an operator’s own advertising, from video spots to digital banners.
  • Event sponsorships: brand presence at concerts, album launches or after-parties connected to the artist.
  • Sponsored livestreams: live broadcasts in which the artist plays or interacts with the platform in real time.

Not every format is available or permitted for every gambling company. What is allowed depends on the platform, the operator’s licence and the jurisdiction.

How Sponsorships Differ From Organic Artist Content

Not every mention of gambling is an ad. An artist might reference a casino in a lyric, talk about a poker night in an interview or post from a trip to Las Vegas without any commercial relationship. That is organic content: the artist’s own choice, unpaid and unprompted.

Sponsored content is different. When an artist receives money, a commission, free play credits or other benefits in exchange for promoting a brand, the post becomes advertising, even if it looks exactly like a casual update.

Why Disclosure Matters to Fans

Fans tend to treat an artist’s posts as genuine opinion. That trust is exactly why the law requires transparency. Canada’s Competition Bureau explains that anyone promoting a business must disclose any “material connection” with it. That includes payments, commissions, free products or services, discounts and free trips or event tickets. The disclosure has to be prominent and written in plain language. Tagging a brand, sharing a discount code or posting an affiliate link is unlikely to count as sufficient disclosure on its own.

For gambling content, this goes beyond a technicality. A viewer who believes a star is risking their own money will interpret a big win or loss very differently from one who knows the session is part of a marketing deal.

Can Artists Stream Gambling Content?

Livestreaming has become one of the most direct ways for artists to connect with fans, and gambling streams have been part of that trend. Drake’s appearances on gambling streams alongside Adin Ross brought the format to a mainstream audience. Whether an artist can stream gambling, however, depends on the platform.

Twitch Restrictions and Platform Policies

So, can you stream gambling on Twitch? Only within narrow limits. Twitch’s Community Guidelines prohibit sharing links or affiliate codes to sites that offer slots, roulette or dice games. They also bar streaming or linking to a named list of gambling sites, including stake.com, rollbit.com, duelbits.com, roobet.com, blaze.com and gamdom.com. Free or social versions of those sites fall under the same ban, and so do their logos. The rule applies whether or not the streamer personally gambles.

These rules are not a blanket ban on gambling topics. The same guidelines state that Twitch currently permits broadcasting sites focused on fantasy sports, sports betting and poker. Each platform sets its own policies, so artists and their teams need to check the specific rules before planning any gambling-related stream.

What Canadian Advertising Rules Mean for Celebrity Partnerships

In Canada, gambling is regulated at the provincial level, and rules differ from one province to another. Ontario is the clearest example of a regulated, privately operated online market. It opened to registered private operators in April 2022 under the oversight of the Alcohol and Gaming Commission of Ontario (AGCO).

In 2023, the AGCO announced amendments to its Registrar’s Standards for Internet Gaming, which took effect on February 28, 2024. The changes ban active and retired athletes from igaming advertising in Ontario, except when they promote responsible gambling. They also restrict the use of celebrities, role models, social media influencers and entertainers who would likely be expected to appeal to minors.

Nationally, the Canadian Gaming Association’s Code for Responsible Gaming Advertising came into force on January 1, 2026. Ad Standards Canada handles complaints under it.

Restrictions Involving Younger Audiences

Ontario’s test focuses on the audience, not the person. The earlier standard targeted content with a “primary appeal” to minors. The updated wording covers anyone likely to appeal to minors, which is a much broader net.

For musicians, that matters. A rapper whose fan base skews toward teenagers may be a far riskier choice for an Ontario operator than an artist whose audience is mostly adults. The rules do not ban every celebrity from gambling advertising, and they apply to operators registered in Ontario rather than automatically across Canada. They do, however, make an artist’s audience profile a compliance issue, not just a marketing metric.

The Reputation Risks of Gambling Partnerships

A gambling deal can be lucrative, but it also links an artist’s name to a product that carries real financial risk for some fans. Asking what the risks of gambling are is not only a question for players. It is also a question for artists deciding what they want to be associated with. If a campaign draws criticism, a lawsuit or a regulatory complaint, the artist’s name is often the one in the headline, even when the operator wrote the script.

Fan trust is hard to rebuild. Audiences that feel misled about a paid relationship, or feel pushed toward risky behaviour, may question the artist’s other endorsements, and even their music.

Why Entertainment and Advertising Must Remain Distinguishable

How a gambling ad is framed matters as much as who appears in it. In a 2026 decision published by Ad Standards Canada, a panel reviewed two social media ads in which influencers described using an online gaming app to escape boredom.

The ads mentioned a low deposit threshold and instant payouts. The panel found that the ads presented gambling as relief from boredom, which breaches the CGA Code’s social responsibility provisions. The advertiser removed the videos.

The Future of Sponsorships in Hip-Hop

Brand partnerships will remain central to how artists build their businesses, and gambling companies are likely to keep looking for cultural figures with large followings. The terms of those relationships, however, are changing. Platform rules, provincial standards and industry codes now shape what an artist can say, where they can say it and to whom.

A few principles are becoming essential for any long-term brand relationship: clear disclosure of paid connections, compliance with the rules of each market and platform, an honest understanding of who is actually listening, and messaging that does not mislead fans about risk.

An artist’s commercial value has always depended on reach. Increasingly, it depends just as much on trust. In a business built on authenticity, how a partnership is handled can matter more to an artist’s reputation than the size of the deal.

item.title: DJ Khaled Reveals 75-Pound Loss As Wegovy Campaign Expands
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: DJ Khaled puts a number on his weight-loss journey as Novo Nordisk builds a new campaign around his personal experience.
item.content:encoded:
DJ Khaled says he has lost 75 pounds after a year on Wegovy, putting a number behind his transformation as he expands his partnership with the drugmaker.

Novo Nordisk announced the new campaign. Khaled will discuss fatherhood, his daily routine and the performance that pushed him to seek medical help.

“I’ve been taking Wegovy for a year now and lost 75 pounds, or about 25% of my body weight. My progress, it’s something I’m proud of — not just for myself, but what taking these steps means for my family. Being a father, being a husband, doing this for the people who depend on me — that’s the real major key. I’m grateful for the journey, grateful for my family, and grateful to share this chapter with the people who’ve supported me from day one,” DJ Khaled said.

Khaled described struggling during a show about a year earlier. A friend’s observation helped convince him that walking and golf alone weren’t doing enough.

He consulted his doctor and added the medication alongside changes to his diet. The new promotion centers on his own experience, not a promise that everyone taking the prescription will get the same results.

Khaled has been turning his health goals into public campaigns for years. In January 2018, Weight Watchers named him a social media ambassador after Roc Nation introduced him to the company. He shared his progress on its Freestyle program across Snapchat, Instagram, Facebook and Twitter.

“I started a new chapter of more goals, more wins, and more blessings. And managing my weight is part of it — so, no more gatekeeping. I partnered with Wegovy to bring people fully behind the scenes into my day-to-day routine and let them know they’ve got options. So, if someone is thinking about Wegovy, they should talk to their doctor and figure out what’s best for them,” DJ Khaled said.

That partnership also followed him on the road. The companies launched Khaled’s Kitchen Tour in March 2018, bringing a food truck with recipes inspired by his personal chef to concert stops. The pop-ups connected his touring schedule with the effort to change his eating habits.

This isn’t Khaled’s first appearance for Wegovy. He participated in its Super Bowl commercial earlier this year, then responded to criticism of his weight-loss partnerships by emphasizing the work he was putting in.

At that point, his public updates highlighted long walks and rounds of golf without a cart. The latest announcement adds a specific account of medication use and how much weight he says he lost.

Khaled began taking Wegovy in late 2025, according to Novo Nordisk.

item.title: EXCLUSIVE: 6ix9ine Faces Kooda B Lawsuit Over Snitch Claims & Death Threats
item.dc:creator: Grouchy Greg Watkins (@GrouchyGreg)
item.description: 6ix9ine's former friend Kooda B takes their feud to federal court, alleging false accusations derailed his comeback.
item.content:encoded:
6ix9ine faces a federal defamation lawsuit from Kooda B, who says his former friend’s repeated snitch accusations cost him work and triggered death threats online.

Filed October 16 in New York’s Eastern District, the 48-page complaint seeks more than $150,000 in damages. Kooda B accuses 6ix9ine of falsely portraying him as a federal informant and linking him to crimes against the rapper and his family.

“At no time did Plaintiff identify the shooter,” the complaint states. “At no time did Plaintiff engage in a proffer or information-for-plea exchange.”

That dispute reaches back to a friendship built before the Nine Trey racketeering case. Kooda B, a Brooklyn rapper from Brownsville, became friends with 6ix9ine through music in 2017 and 2018, according to the filing. 6ix9ine named his 2017 single “Kooda” after him, and Kooda B appeared in its video.

Their connection later became part of a federal criminal prosecution. Kooda B pleaded guilty on June 3, 2019, to assault with a dangerous weapon in aid of racketeering. Federal prosecutors said he accepted money from 6ix9ine and helped arrange the June 2, 2018, Times Square shooting targeting Chief Keef.

Kooda B’s role was organizing the shooting, not pulling the trigger. Chief Keef was not injured, and the complaint says another person fired the weapon. The conviction was not for attempted murder.

Judge Paul Engelmayer sentenced Kooda B to 54 months in prison on December 1, 2020. His sentence also included three years of supervised release, according to the Justice Department.

The lawsuit argues that admitting his own conduct during a guilty plea did not make Kooda B an informant. It says 6ix9ine had already supplied investigators with the information used to prosecute him.

The complaint points to 6ix9ine’s December 2019 sentencing, where it says the judge identified Kooda B among defendants who pleaded guilty without cooperating. It also cites prosecutors’ sentencing submissions to argue that Kooda B withheld the identities of others involved, rather than trading their names for a lighter sentence.

The complaint traces the disputed statements through Clubhouse, interviews and livestreams. It quotes 6ix9ine saying on Clubhouse, “Kooda B told the feds who really shot the gun.” Kooda B’s lawyers call that statement false.

Kooda B also disputes suggestions that he kidnapped, robbed or stole from 6ix9ine. The filing says those accusations wrongly fold him into conduct involving other people from the federal case.

“Plaintiff never kidnapped, robbed, threatened, extorted, wiretapped, or stole from Defendant Hernandez, his family, or any promoter,” the complaint states.

The suit says the resulting harassment damaged Kooda B’s music career, cost him professional relationships and left him fearing for his family. Those claims underpin a defamation-per-se count seeking actual and punitive damages, along with an injunction against further unlawful conduct.

Kooda B has requested a jury trial.

item.title: FKA Twigs’ Josephine Baker Audition Brings Director To Tears
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: FKA twigs wins over her filmmaker in an emotional tryout for a biopic about Josephine Baker's artistry and civil rights work.
item.content:encoded:
FKA twigs made Maïmouna Doucouré forget she was watching an audition, not Josephine Baker herself. The director says that performance reduced her to tears during the search for her film’s leading actress.

Doucouré described that turning point in Variety’s new report from the set. She needed someone who could carry demanding dramatic scenes alongside the singing and dancing.

“I literally started crying because suddenly I was seeing Josephine Baker. I completely forgot that I had written the scene,” Doucouré said.

The movie centers on Baker’s 1951 return to America and the segregation awaiting her there. Flashbacks connect that chapter to her childhood, Paris breakthrough and wartime resistance work.

Baker’s life gives the production far more to work with than her stage performances. Born in St. Louis, she worked her way through theater and New York’s Harlem Renaissance before finding an audience in Paris.

Her celebrity later provided cover for dangerous work against the Nazis. While entertaining people connected to the enemy, she gathered information for French military officials and concealed intelligence in musical scores using invisible ink.

The fight against racism continued after the war, when Baker challenged venues that separated their audiences by race. Her refusal to accept those arrangements pressured club owners to admit integrated crowds.

Baker’s story has already drawn another major recording artist toward the screen. AllHipHop reported in 2022 that Janelle Monáe was attached to a separate Baker series, with A24 and Monáe’s Wondaland involved.

That announced television project focused on Baker’s espionage during World War II. Her screen career broke barriers too, as the first Black woman to lead a major motion picture in 1927’s Siren of the Tropics.

Baker later spoke at the 1963 March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. She was among the few women given the opportunity to address the gathering.

Doucouré’s production includes Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor as Baker’s mother and draws on collaboration with Baker’s family in this Studiocanal-backed feature. Twigs has learned French for the part, which also requires her to portray Baker across different ages.

Filming in France and Bulgaria is scheduled to continue through November 13.

item.title: Eminem Reopens His Pre-Slim Shady Archive With ‘Infinite’ EP
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Eminem revisits his Detroit beginnings with a six-track collection, archival film and a vinyl bonus from the Hip Hop Shop.
item.content:encoded:
Eminem is revisiting the recordings he made before his Slim Shady LP with an anniversary release that goes beyond another remix.

His re-released first effort, the Infinite EP arrives with a new mini-documentary, while a vinyl-only freestyle adds another piece of his early Detroit history.

The six-song digital collection landed November 12, exactly 30 years after the debut album that would lead to his worldwide success was released. The label says the accompanying film draws on rare archival footage.

This is a selection from Infinite, not a newly recorded Eminem project. Jake Bass and Mike “Slim” Wilder handled fresh mixes and additional production for the returning tracks.

The EP includes “Infinite,” “It’s O.K.,” “Tonite,” “313,” “Open Mic” and “Never 2 Far.” Denaun Porter produced the original recordings, with Wilder co-producing and Jeff and Mark Bass serving as executive producers.

Long before those sessions, Eminem was recording demos and performing around Detroit. Champtown told AllHipHop in a 2019 interview that dancer Shortcut introduced them while Eminem belonged to the Basement Productions crew.

“I met Eminem through a guy named Shortcut,” Champtown recalled. Their work included “What Color Is Soul” with Chaos Kid and Eminem’s appearance in Champtown’s “Do-Da-Dippity” video.

Champtown also took him to Prince’s Paisley Park studio in 1992. Metro Times’ 2004 profile described footage from that session and their early performances, documenting a relationship that stretched back years before Infinite.

His route to the Bass Brothers began with radio, not Dr. Dre. In a 2000 Mix interview, Eminem recalled cutting demos and rapping on air when Mark Bass heard him.

“Mark heard the shit on the air and called the studio on the spot. We met later that week,” Eminem said.

An attempted Elektra deal went nowhere, and they stopped working together. Eminem said he later financed a single with his income-tax check while building his Detroit reputation. The brothers offered a production deal after reconnecting, laying the groundwork for the independent recordings that reached listeners through Web Entertainment.

The album’s anniversary has prompted an archival return before. AllHipHop covered the title track’s 20th-anniversary remix in November 2016, alongside a documentary about the album’s creation.

That earlier release centered on bringing the title song back into circulation. This edition collects six tracks and gives vinyl buyers an extra performance: “The Hip Hop Shop Freestyle – Feb 17, 1996.”

The original album came through Web Entertainment in limited vinyl and cassette quantities.

Vinyl, CD and cassette editions of the EP follow on February 26, 2027.
